Fig. 1 The city of Curitiba, southern Brazil, and the ten study sites with analyzed buffers. A Brazil (green) and state of Paraná (gray). B Curitiba (green), C study sites and buffers (750 m, 1 km, 1.5 km, and 2 km)

Sampling was carried out one day per month for ten months between August 2017 and May 2018, for a total of ten days of sampling at each site. The sampling period was designed so as to exclude the winter months of June and July when there is minimal bee activity (average temperature of 9.3 °C). Sampling was carried out for six hours per day (9:00 a.m. 03:30 p.m., with a half-hour break) for a total of 60 h per site. No surveys were carried out on cloudy or rainy days due to reduced bee activity. Flower-visiting bees were collected with entomological nets by one collector (LVG). The surveys were carried out within a radius of up to 200 m around the centroid and aimed to visit every flowering plant in the study area during the sampling period. This distance was defined to standardize the sampling area regardless of fragment size, as well as to be a manageable size for a single day of sampling.

We chose to focus on wild bees only, meaning that individuals of the Western honey bee (Apis mellifera) were not collected as including them would jeopardize the sampling and processing of the other specimens. All other specimens collected were pre-pared for identification on entomological pins, dried at temperatures between 40 and 60 °C for three days, labeled, identified, recorded in a database, and finally deposited in the Jesus Santiago Moure Entomologi cal Collection (DZUP) at the Federal University of

We used a Landsat 8 image of the study area, which has a 30 m resolution. The acquisition date was April 25th, 2016 (ID: LC08_L1TP_220078_20160425_2 0170326_01_T1; path: 220; row: 78). The georeferencing image underwent geometric correction and atmospheric correction (DOS1) before the classification procedure. Image classification was performed using the Semi-Automatic Classification Plugin (SCP) (Congedo 2016) with QGIS version 3.10.0 (QGIS Development Team 2019). The resulting landuse map was manually post-processed to correct the minor errors of the semi-automatic classification. We considered five units, defined as follows: urban area, water bodies, forest vegetation, shrub vegetation, and grassland vegetation. The grassland unit includes natural open fields, managed grass, exposed soil, and areas covered with ruderal plants. In this study, four buffers were used to obtain the spatial metrics (750 m, 1 km, 1.5 km, and 2 km) (Fig. 1), defined
![Image block](doc:88854a4/tier:advanced/page:9/block:3)

absent at the most urbanized site, as previously reported by Taura and Laroca (2001). Cuckoo bees depend on the presence of their host and the resources it provides (Rozen 2001; Michener 2007), meaning that they are directly affected by landscape disturbances. Thus, a linear response to environmental metrics can be attenuated in some circumstances. A pair of long-term studies by Martins et al. (2013) and Cardoso and Gonçalves (2018) monitored Sites 10 and 3, respectively, and did not find evidence of declines in kleptoparasites. As discussed by Sheffield et al. (2013), kleptoparasites can be indicative of the status of the total bee assemblage and, as expected, they were more affected by the metrics evaluated than the bee community at large (assumed by the higher intercept values), indicating that monitoring in urban areas should also focus on these bees.
